list.listitem: The specialty board position statement from the American Academy of Pediatrics (also endorsed by the American College of Obstetrics and Gynecology) states that benefits of neonatal circumcision outweigh the risks and that the procedure's benefits justify access to it for families who choose circumcision. However, the primary indication for circumcision remains parental preference.

The possible benefits of neonatal circumcision include a protective effect against penile cancer, decreased risk of genital HPV, and a decreasd HPV transmission to females from circumcised men and a decreased risk of HIV acquisition by heterosexual men.

In a RCT of over 3,000 HIV-negative men aged 15 to 49 years, at 24 month follow-up those randomized to circumcision had reduced incidence of new herpes simplex virus type 2 (HSV-2) infections (7.8% vs. 10.3%, NNT = 40) and reduced prevalence of infection with high-risk human papillomavirus (HPV) subtypes (18% vs. 27.9%).

Based on 3 RCTs conducted in Africa, authors of a Cochrane review concluded that there is strong evidence that medical male circumcision reduces the acquisition of HIV by heterosexual men by between 38% and 66% over 24 months. A recent systematic review and meta-analysis of observational studies performed for the World Health Organizations confirmed this benefit.

A Cochrane review of 21 observational studies found no statistically significant reduction in HIV transmission among MSM in general. A subgroup analysis of 7 studies containing 3465 participants found a significant effect in men who primarily practice insertive anal sex (OR 0.27; 95% CI, 0.17-0.44).

Neonatal circumcision reduces the incidence of UTI in boys. A 2005 meta-analysis showed a NNT of 111. Given the approximately 1% complication rate of the procedure, the authors conclude that this benefit does not outweigh the risks.
Abnormal or ambiguous male genitalia.
Any illness or injury that would supersede an elective procedure.
Ensure the infant is at least 12 to 24 hours old, that he has urinated, and obtain parental consent.
Restrain the infant.
Inspect the penis for abnormalities, and verify normal position of the urethral meatus.
Cleanse the penis and scrotum, and use aseptic technique.

Use anesthesia: Either dorsal penile nerve block or penile ring block are both effective. A systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs found that dorsal penile nerve block was more effective at relieving pain from circumcision than EMLA cream. EMLA cream decreases pain compared to placebo.
Sucrose administered orally on a pacifier is not effective in reducing pain. Avoid taking too much penile skin by not pulling the prepuce too tight. Conversely, avoid leaving too much foreskin by not leaving the prepuce too loose.

Option 1: Gomco clamp.
Separate the prepuce from the glans, releasing all adhesions with a blunt probe while holding the foreskin at 10 and 2 o'clock with hemostats. After the adhesions have been released, use a straight hemostat to firmly crimp approximately three fourths of the length of the foreskin at the 12 o'clock position for about 30 seconds. Remove the straight hemostat and cut the foreskin down the center of the crimped line being careful to remain within the margins of the crushed skin (). Retract the foreskin and place the correct size bell over the glans of the penis (). Then re-approximate the skin edges over the bell with a hemostat, or a sterile safety pin, to hold the Gomco bell in place. Position the bell stem through the Gomco ring and clamp a hemostat through the ring onto the foreskin (). After hemostats have been placed and the bell has been lightly seated in the ring then the first hemostat can be removed and the foreskin can be pulled through the ring beyond the apex of the original clamp sight. After the foreskin has been uniformly positioned beyond the apex of the incision, clamp the bell stem into the Gomco and tighten the clamp. Then trim the foreskin off of the Gomco with a scalpel (). Be extremely vigilant as to the position of the scalpel! This is where the most serious complications can occur. Remove the clamp and check for bleeding. Cover the glans with petrolatum, re-diaper the patient. Record the next urination. Counsel the parents to use petrolatum on the glans after each diaper change for the next two weeks.

Option 2: Plastibell.
Place the Plastibell string in a loose circle around the base of the penis utilizing a half hitch. Separate the prepuce from the glans, releasing all adhesions with a blunt probe while holding the foreskin at 10 and 2 o'clock with hemostats. After the adhesions have been released, use a straight hemostat to firmly crimp about approximately three fourths of the length of the foreskin at the 12 o'clock position for about 30 seconds. Remove the straight hemostat and cut the foreskin down the center of the crimped line being careful to remain within the margins of the crushed skin (). Retract the foreskin and place the correct size Plastibell over the glans of the penis. Re-approximate the skin edges over the Plastibell, and remove one hemostat. Hold the cut skin edges in approximation with a single hemostat. The second hemostat may be used to control the Plastibell by clamping it across the stem. Position the Plastibell so that the grooved ring is below the proximal end of the incision. Place the string over the groove, but not tightly. Ensure that the string and groove are beyond the apex of the incision. When the foreskin is uniformly positioned distal to the string, tighten the string. Tie a square knot in the string, and remove the hemostats. Cut the foreskin within 1/8 of an inch of the distal side of the string with a pair of scissors circumferentially () and remove the foreskin. Then trim the loose ends of the string. Finally, break off the stem of the Plastibell by bending the stem back and forth while holding the ring at the corona of the glans. This will leave a plastic ring, a string and the cut edge of the foreskin. Check for bleeding. Cover the glans with petrolatum, and re-diaper the patient. Record the next urination. The cut edge of the foreskin should become necrotic, turn black and fall off along with the ring and string in about one week.

Option 3: Mogen.
Separate the prepuce from the glans, releasing all adhesions with a blunt probe while holding the foreskin at 10 and 2 o'clock with hemostats. After all of the adhesions have been released, remove the hemostats and place a straight hemostat on the foreskin at 12 o'clock to a depth of 5 mm distal of the corona of the glans. Using the hemostat, pull the prepuce upward, causing the glans to retract. Position the Mogen clamp so that it is distal to the glans penis but proximal to the hemostat. Close the clamp partially then recheck the clamp position. After ensuring proper Mogen placement, clamp the Mogen tightly and cut the foreskin off flush to the clamp with a scalpel (). After the clamp has been in place for 1 to 2 minutes, remove the clamp. Separate the foreskin and expose the glans penis by applying pressure downward along the direction of the shaft of the penis. Remove any remaining adhesions using gauze or a blunt probe. Check for bleeding. Cover the glans with petrolatum, re-diaper the patient. Record the next urination. Counsel the parents to use petrolatum on the glans after each diaper change for the next two weeks.
Total incidence of complications is 0.22%.
Bleeding incidence of 0.18%. Use pressure tamponade, silver nitrate, and Monsel solution to treat.
Injury incidence of 0.04%. If injury occurs, stop the procedure. Stop any bleeding caused by the injury and call for a urosurgical consult.

Separation of the skin from the membrane. This can result from the clamp not compressing the two layers (skin and membrane) together adequately. This can occur partially or completely where the skin piles at the bottom of the penis with only the membrane still adherent to the shaft. In either case, the treatment is to remain calm and suture the two together again with interrupted absorbable suture just below the glans where the original cut was made.
Infection described as cellulitis of the penis had an incidence of 0.0008%. Treat with good wound care and judicious antibiotic use.

A RCT found that newborns circumcised with the Mogen clamp, compared to the Gomco, experienced fewer physiologic signs of pain (salivary cortisol levels, heart rate, and mean arterial blood pressure) but had equivalent clinical pain scores.
Ensure urination and hemostasis prior to hospital discharge.
Routine well child exams.
